items.prompt: A web application routes requests by hostname and URL path to different target groups. Which load balancer is the direct fit?
constraints: The workload is HTTP or HTTPS.
Routing needs layer-7 attributes.
Targets may represent separate application services.

options.text: Use an Application Load Balancer with listener rules and target groups for host- or path-based HTTP routing.
Use a Gateway Load Balancer because it routes web requests by URL path through security appliances.
Use a Network Load Balancer because transport-level forwarding evaluates HTTP host headers automatically.
Use Route 53 weighted records because DNS can inspect every URL path in an HTTP request.

feedback.Reason: ALB provides layer-7 listener rules for HTTP host and path routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Application Load Balancer listeners can evaluate HTTP attributes and forward requests to target groups.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team maps host and path contracts to services and applies target health and authorization behavior per listener rule.
Details.errorCorrection: GWLB inserts appliances, NLB operates at transport level, and DNS cannot inspect the full HTTP path for each request.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Layer-7 routing adds application-aware behavior and header or protocol considerations that must be tested.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: GWLB is for transparent insertion of virtual appliances, not URL routing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: NLB does not provide the same host- and path-based application routing contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS routing does not evaluate each HTTP URL path.

items.prompt: A partner requires a stable IP address and the service accepts TCP without HTTP-aware routing. Which load balancer should be evaluated first?
constraints: The protocol is TCP.
The endpoint needs stable addressing.
The service does not need URL or host routing.

options.text: Evaluate a Network Load Balancer for transport-level TCP forwarding and the required static addressing behavior.
Use an Application Load Balancer because all load balancers provide identical layer-4 and addressing behavior.
Use Gateway Load Balancer because it is the general replacement for every TCP service.
Use a CloudFront distribution because edge caching provides a stable origin IP for arbitrary TCP sessions.

feedback.Reason: NLB is designed for high-performance transport-level forwarding and supports static IP use cases.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Network Load Balancer handles TCP or other supported transport protocols and exposes network-level behavior appropriate to the requirement.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team verifies listener protocol, target health, source behavior, and the address contract with the partner.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB is application-aware, GWLB inserts appliances, and CloudFront is not a general arbitrary TCP endpoint.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: NLB provides less application routing than ALB, so the choice depends on the protocol and address contract.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ALB and NLB have different protocol and address behavior; they are not interchangeable.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GWLB is specialized for appliance insertion rather than general service forwarding.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront does not replace a general TCP load balancer for arbitrary sessions.

items.prompt: All traffic to an application must pass through a fleet of third-party firewalls without changing the application endpoints. Which service is designed for this insertion pattern?
constraints: The appliances are virtual network functions.
Traffic should be transparently steered through them.
The service must scale and health-check appliance targets.

options.text: Use Gateway Load Balancer with appliance target groups and endpoint-based traffic steering for transparent inspection or processing.
Use ALB path rules to send each HTTP URL through a firewall appliance as an application response.
Use NLB source-IP hashing as a substitute for appliance insertion and inspection.
Use S3 replication because replicated objects can be inspected as live network packets.

feedback.Reason: GWLB is purpose-built to deploy, scale, and integrate virtual appliances into network paths.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Gateway Load Balancer uses GENEVE-based appliance integration and endpoint patterns for traffic steering through target appliances.
Details.scenarioApplication: The network routes selected traffic to a GWLB endpoint, and the appliance fleet has health, scale, and return-path behavior defined.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB URL routing is not transparent network insertion, NLB hashing is forwarding rather than inspection, and S3 is storage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Appliance insertion adds routing, symmetry, health, and throughput considerations that must be validated end to end.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ALB routes HTTP requests but does not provide transparent network appliance insertion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Hashing distributes connections and does not itself inspect or insert a firewall.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Object replication has no relationship to live packet processing.

items.prompt: A web service wants to terminate TLS centrally, route by path, and forward to HTTP targets inside a VPC. Which design should be evaluated?
constraints: The client protocol is HTTPS.
The load balancer can own the public certificate.
Targets are private and can receive the selected internal protocol.

options.text: Use an HTTPS listener on an Application Load Balancer with a managed certificate and path or host rules, then secure the target connection as required.
Use a Network Load Balancer because it must inspect URL paths after terminating every HTTP request.
Terminate TLS in every browser and send the certificate private key to each application target.
Use Route 53 as the TLS terminator because DNS records carry certificates to targets.

feedback.Reason: ALB combines HTTPS listener termination with application-aware routing and private target delivery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The listener can use an ACM certificate and forward requests to target groups after evaluating application routing rules.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team defines client-to-ALB and ALB-to-target encryption, certificate renewal, and target security-group access.
Details.errorCorrection: NLB is not selected for URL routing, private keys should not be distributed to targets unnecessarily, and DNS does not terminate TLS.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: TLS termination reduces target certificate management but requires careful trust, header, and re-encryption decisions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: NLB transport behavior does not provide the requested path routing contract.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Distributing private keys increases exposure and is not required for centralized termination.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Route 53 resolves names and does not terminate TLS sessions.

items.prompt: A service requires the backend to see the original TLS session and perform its own certificate and protocol negotiation. Which load-balancer behavior should be considered?
constraints: The target owns TLS policy.
The load balancer should not terminate the session.
The protocol is compatible with transport-level forwarding.

options.text: Evaluate a Network Load Balancer TLS pass-through or transport listener design that preserves the target's TLS responsibility, with explicit certificate and health behavior.
Use an ALB HTTPS listener and discard the target's TLS boundary because all clients require the same certificate.
Use a DNS alias and assume it preserves a session through a changing target.
Use GWLB because every TLS session must pass through a security appliance.

feedback.Reason: NLB supports transport-oriented designs where the target retains the TLS session responsibility.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Transport forwarding can preserve the connection to the target, while the target handles its certificate, cipher, and application TLS behavior.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team verifies client source behavior, target certificates, health checks, and any need for SNI or end-to-end encryption.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB termination changes the TLS boundary, DNS does not preserve a session, and GWLB is not selected merely because TLS exists.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pass-through preserves target control but distributes certificate and TLS operations across the target fleet.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ALB termination moves the TLS boundary to the load balancer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS selects an endpoint but does not preserve a live session.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: GWLB is for appliance insertion and is not required for every TLS workload.

items.prompt: A browser application uses WebSockets and needs host-based routing to multiple services. Which load balancer is a candidate?
constraints: The workload begins as HTTP or HTTPS.
The connection upgrades to WebSocket.
Routing must distinguish services by host.

options.text: Evaluate an Application Load Balancer with WebSocket support and host-based listener rules, then test connection timeout and target-drain behavior.
Use S3 website hosting because object storage maintains WebSocket sessions and host routing.
Use Route 53 weighted routing for every message sent over the already-established WebSocket connection.
Use GWLB because WebSockets are network appliances rather than application connections.

feedback.Reason: ALB supports application-layer HTTP connection patterns including WebSocket upgrades and host routing.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The ALB listener handles the initial HTTP request and maintains the upgraded connection to a healthy target according to its configuration.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team sets idle timeout, deployment draining, authentication, and target ownership for long-lived connections.
Details.errorCorrection: S3 website hosting is not a general WebSocket service, DNS does not route messages within a live connection, and GWLB is for appliances.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long-lived connections affect scale-in and target draining, so connection lifecycle needs explicit testing.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Object hosting does not provide the required dynamic WebSocket target routing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS is consulted before a connection and cannot route individual messages within it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A WebSocket is an application connection, not automatically an appliance workload.

items.prompt: A gaming service uses UDP and needs low-overhead connection forwarding. Which family should be evaluated?
constraints: The protocol is UDP.
The service does not need HTTP path routing.
Target health and capacity remain required.

options.text: Evaluate a Network Load Balancer with the supported UDP listener and target health configuration.
Use an Application Load Balancer because all protocols are interpreted as HTTP at the listener.
Use CloudFront because CDN caching can forward every UDP packet to the game server.
Use an SQS queue because messages in a queue preserve a real-time UDP session.

feedback.Reason: NLB is the load-balancer family for transport protocols such as UDP where application-layer HTTP routing is not the contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: NLB listeners and target groups support transport-oriented forwarding and health behavior for compatible protocols.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect validates packet flow, idle or connection behavior, target health, and game-specific latency requirements.
Details.errorCorrection: ALB is HTTP-oriented, CloudFront is not a generic UDP proxy, and SQS is asynchronous messaging rather than a session forwarder.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Transport forwarding leaves more protocol behavior to the targets and may require separate protection and observability.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: ALB does not replace an NLB transport listener for UDP.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFront does not forward arbitrary real-time UDP sessions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: SQS changes the interaction to asynchronous messages and does not preserve a live session.

items.prompt: A provider exposes a private TCP service to consumer VPCs through AWS PrivateLink. Which endpoint-side load-balancer family is commonly evaluated?
constraints: The provider service is private.
Consumers should not need broad network peering.
The provider controls target health and capacity.

options.text: Evaluate a Network Load Balancer as the provider service endpoint behind an interface endpoint, with explicit listener and target behavior.
Use a public ALB and ask consumers to allow the provider's entire internet address range.
Use Route 53 private zones alone because DNS creates a PrivateLink service without an endpoint.
Use an S3 bucket policy because object access policies expose arbitrary private TCP services.

feedback.Reason: NLB is a standard provider-side integration point for PrivateLink endpoint services and private TCP exposure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: PrivateLink uses interface endpoints to connect consumers to an endpoint service exposed by a provider, with the provider load balancer and targets owning service health.
Details.scenarioApplication: The provider publishes the service, limits principals, and monitors endpoint connections and target health without opening broad routes.
Details.errorCorrection: A public ALB expands exposure, DNS does not create the endpoint service, and S3 policies do not expose network listeners.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: PrivateLink requires endpoint, principal, DNS, quota, and provider-service lifecycle planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Public exposure and broad ranges violate the private connectivity requirement.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS can name an endpoint but cannot create the PrivateLink service or data path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: S3 authorization applies to objects and not arbitrary network services.

items.prompt: A target returns a successful process health response but cannot serve application traffic because a local dependency is unavailable. How should health be designed?
constraints: A target must be usable, not merely running.
A shared dependency failure should not create a replacement storm.
The load balancer must stop sending traffic to an unusable target.

options.text: Define an application readiness endpoint that reflects local serving ability, separate it from deep shared-dependency alarms, and use it for target routing.
Return success from every health endpoint and let user requests reveal target failure.
Use only EC2 status checks because load balancers cannot evaluate application health.
Make the health endpoint perform a full production transaction on every probe.

feedback.Reason: Health checks should represent whether the target can serve traffic while avoiding a probe design that turns shared failure into churn.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A readiness contract can remove a locally unusable target; broader dependency health should be observed and handled at the service level.
Details.scenarioApplication: The target checks its own process and required local state, while downstream outage behavior uses alarms, limits, and explicit responses.
Details.errorCorrection: Always-success health hides failure, EC2 status is not application readiness, and full transactions on every probe add load and side effects.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The shallower the check, the more failure is discovered by requests; the deeper it is, the greater storm risk.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Always-success checks send traffic to targets that cannot serve it.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Instance status does not prove application readiness.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Health probes should be safe, bounded, and free of destructive business side effects.

items.prompt: An API is used only by workloads inside a VPC and should not have a public internet entry point. Which load-balancer placement is appropriate?
constraints: Clients use private network paths.
The API does not require public ingress.
The service still needs target health and scaling.

options.text: Use an internal load balancer in private subnets with security-group or network controls that allow only the intended clients.
Use an internet-facing load balancer and rely on a secret URL because public endpoints are simpler to secure.
Use a public IP on every target and omit the load balancer because private clients do not need health routing.
Use CloudFront as the only private VPC ingress because every distribution is automatically internal.

feedback.Reason: An internal load balancer provides the required private entry point while retaining health-aware distribution.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Internal load balancers resolve to private addresses and can route clients to healthy targets within the selected network design.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect controls client routes, security groups, DNS, and target exposure so the API is not directly internet-addressable.
Details.errorCorrection: A secret public URL is still public, direct targets lose a health and ownership boundary, and CloudFront is not automatically a private VPC ingress.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Private load balancing still needs DNS, cross-network connectivity, authorization, and target capacity planning.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A secret URL does not remove public exposure or scanning risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Direct targets bypass health-aware distribution and expand the client-to-instance boundary.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront distributions are not a substitute for every internal VPC load-balancer path.

items.prompt: The application must record the original client IP for audit and rate limiting. Which design concern should be verified?
constraints: Traffic passes through a load balancer.
The application must distinguish trusted forwarding metadata from client input.
The recorded identity affects security decisions.

options.text: Use the load balancer's documented client-address behavior or forwarding headers, restrict who can reach targets, and ensure the application trusts the header only from the load balancer path.
Trust any X-Forwarded-For value supplied directly by a public client because headers cannot be changed in transit.
Use the target's private IP as the client identity because it is stable for every user.
Disable source logging because load balancing makes client identity impossible to preserve.

feedback.Reason: Client identity through a proxy is a trust-boundary decision, not merely a header-reading detail.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: The load balancer can add forwarding metadata, but targets must be protected so clients cannot bypass or forge the trusted path.
Details.scenarioApplication: The application validates proxy topology, parses the documented header, and records the identity with appropriate privacy and audit controls.
Details.errorCorrection: Public clients can forge headers, target IP is not user identity, and a proxy does not make preservation impossible.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Forwarded identity requires infrastructure and application agreement and should not be used for authorization without a trusted path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Untrusted clients can submit arbitrary forwarding headers.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: The target address identifies infrastructure, not the original client.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Load balancers provide documented mechanisms for forwarding client address information.

items.prompt: A deployment must remove a target without cutting active requests abruptly. Which behavior is important?
constraints: Requests may be long-lived.
New requests should stop reaching the target.
Active requests need a bounded chance to complete.

options.text: Use target deregistration or connection-draining behavior with an appropriate timeout, then verify application shutdown and retry semantics.
Terminate the target first and let clients discover the change through connection resets.
Keep the target registered forever so deployments never affect active connections.
Return a successful response from the load balancer for requests that were never processed.

feedback.Reason: Draining separates admission of new requests from completion of existing connections during replacement.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Deregistration delay gives active connections time to finish while the load balancer stops assigning new work to the target.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team chooses a timeout from request duration and ensures the application can close or retry safely after the bound.
Details.errorCorrection: Abrupt termination causes failures, permanent registration blocks replacement, and fake responses violate the request contract.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Long drain delays rollout and scale-in, while short drain can interrupt legitimate work; the objective sets the value.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Immediate termination cuts active requests and increases user-visible errors.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Never deregistering a target prevents controlled deployment and recovery.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: The balancer cannot truthfully complete work the target never processed.

items.prompt: A target group spans two Availability Zones, but one zone currently has fewer targets and higher traffic. Which behavior must be verified?
constraints: Zone-level target distribution affects capacity.
The service has an availability objective.
Cross-zone behavior and data-transfer implications matter.

options.text: Verify the selected load balancer's cross-zone distribution, target capacity per zone, health behavior, and traffic or cost implications under zone imbalance.
Assume every load balancer always distributes traffic equally across all instances regardless of configuration.
Remove targets from the healthy zone so both zones have equal target counts even if capacity falls below demand.
Use DNS round robin as a replacement for target health and load-balancer distribution.

feedback.Reason: Zone and target distribution behavior is service-specific and must be matched to the capacity and failure objective.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Load balancer distribution, health checks, zone placement, and target capacity determine how traffic behaves during imbalance or zone loss.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team load-tests normal and degraded zone states and confirms that remaining targets and quotas can absorb the traffic.
Details.errorCorrection: Equal distribution is not automatic in every mode, removing healthy capacity is unsafe, and DNS lacks target-level health and balancing semantics.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Cross-zone distribution can improve utilization but may change data transfer, locality, and failure behavior.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Distribution behavior depends on load balancer type and configuration.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing healthy capacity worsens the failure and demand margin.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS cannot replace per-target health and connection distribution.

items.prompt: A service has rising latency but the team cannot tell whether the load balancer, target, or client is responsible. Which evidence should be collected?
constraints: The path includes a load balancer and multiple targets.
Latency has a service objective.
The evidence must distinguish queueing, target response, and connection behavior.

options.text: Correlate load-balancer request, target-response, connection, rejection, health, and application metrics with request traces and target identity.
Collect only aggregate EC2 CPU because load balancer metrics cannot explain latency.
Disable access logs to reduce latency and infer the cause from user complaints.
Replace the load balancer immediately without comparing target and listener evidence.

feedback.Reason: Load-balancer diagnosis needs path-level evidence that separates connection, routing, target, and application time.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Access and service metrics can show target response time, rejected connections, unhealthy targets, and request volume alongside application traces.
Details.scenarioApplication: Operators identify whether to change listener, target capacity, application code, or downstream dependency rather than guessing.
Details.errorCorrection: CPU-only metrics miss network and target behavior, disabling evidence hides the issue, and replacement without diagnosis can repeat it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Logging and tracing cost resources, so sampling and retention should match the operational objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: CPU does not identify listener, connection, target, or network latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing evidence reduces diagnosis and does not fix latency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Replacement without a cause can increase risk and leave the bottleneck unchanged.

items.prompt: A service must support HTTP health checks for one target group and raw TLS connections for another. What should the architect decide?
constraints: The target protocols differ.
Each target group needs an appropriate health check.
The load balancer and listener must support the selected contracts.

options.text: Select listener and target-group protocols per workload, using ALB for HTTP-aware paths and NLB where transport-level TLS forwarding is required, then test health semantics.
Force both workloads through an HTTP listener because protocol conversion always preserves application behavior.
Use one health check type for every target regardless of protocol or response behavior.
Expose both target groups directly and let clients choose the protocol without a load-balancer contract.

feedback.Reason: The load-balancer choice follows the protocol and routing contract of each workload rather than forcing unrelated services through one listener.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB and NLB expose different listener and target protocol behavior; health checks must be valid for the target service.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect maps each service to the least complex compatible listener and retains target isolation and monitoring.
Details.errorCorrection: Forced HTTP can terminate or change a raw TLS contract, one health check cannot fit every protocol, and direct exposure bypasses the boundary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Multiple load-balancer types add components, but a mismatched protocol boundary creates correctness and security failures.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Protocol conversion can change the TLS or application boundary and is not universally transparent.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Health checks must match target protocol and readiness semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Direct targets remove shared health, security, and capacity control.

items.prompt: Targets should accept traffic only from the load balancer and not from clients that discover their private addresses. Which control expresses this?
constraints: Targets are in private subnets.
The load balancer is the intended source.
Security must follow the tier boundary.

options.text: Allow target listener traffic from the load balancer's security group or documented source path, and deny direct client paths with network and routing controls.
Allow the target port from all VPC CIDRs because private addresses are automatically trusted.
Put targets in the same security group as every client so the load balancer does not need a rule.
Use a public target address and depend on the load balancer to hide it from network scanners.

feedback.Reason: The target security boundary should trust the intended load-balancer path, not every possible network source.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Security-group references or equivalent source restrictions limit inbound target traffic to the load-balancer boundary.
Details.scenarioApplication: Clients reach the load balancer, which reaches targets on the service port; direct target access is not a supported route.
Details.errorCorrection: Private CIDRs still contain unintended principals, shared client groups broaden access, and a public address does not hide a target.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Source references and routing must be kept aligned during migrations and cross-VPC designs.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A VPC CIDR includes more sources than the intended load balancer.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A shared group weakens least privilege and makes client access too broad.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Public target exposure increases attack surface and cannot be hidden reliably by the balancer.

items.prompt: A small HTTP service needs only one stable endpoint and simple target distribution; it has no path routing or appliance requirement. What should the architect do?
constraints: The service is simple HTTP.
There is no need for layer-7 rules beyond basic forwarding.
Operational simplicity matters.

options.text: Choose the simplest load-balancer type that satisfies the HTTP, health, security, and address requirements, and avoid adding appliance or advanced routing features without a need.
Use every load-balancer family in series because more layers always improve availability.
Use GWLB by default because its specialized behavior is safest for every application.
Expose each target publicly because a load balancer is unnecessary when traffic is low.

feedback.Reason: Load-balancer selection should satisfy the actual protocol and operational contract without unnecessary components.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB or another compatible simple choice may be sufficient; the architect verifies requirements instead of selecting by feature count.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team documents protocol, routing, health, security, and future growth requirements and chooses one canonical boundary.
Details.errorCorrection: Chaining families adds failure and cost surface, GWLB is specialized, and public targets remove health and security control.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A simpler choice may limit future routing or protocol features, so growth assumptions should be explicit.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Extra load-balancer layers create more dependencies and do not automatically improve availability.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GWLB is not a general default for application forwarding.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Low traffic does not eliminate the need for target health and security boundaries.

items.prompt: Which evidence is strongest when selecting between ALB, NLB, and GWLB for a new service?
constraints: The service protocol and traffic path are known.
The design has security, availability, and scale objectives.
The choice should remain reviewable after launch.

options.text: Map protocol, routing layer, source-address, TLS, appliance, health, capacity, failure, PrivateLink, and operational requirements to one supported load-balancer contract.
Choose the family with the most features regardless of protocol or traffic path.
Choose based only on the service name because similar names imply identical behavior.
Choose the cheapest hourly option before measuring target, data-transfer, and operational costs.

feedback.Reason: The correct load balancer follows the end-to-end traffic and operating contract, not a feature-count or price shortcut.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: ALB, NLB, and GWLB optimize for different layers and integration patterns; the mapping makes trade-offs explicit.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architecture record includes listener and target protocols, health, security groups, deployment draining, quotas, and failure tests.
Details.errorCorrection: More features can be irrelevant, names do not define behavior, and hourly price excludes traffic and operational impact.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A precise choice avoids both underpowered protocol handling and unnecessary layers.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Feature count does not prove compatibility or operational fit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Similar service names do not imply identical layers or behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Hourly price alone ignores data transfer, capacity, health, and operations.
